title: All the letter-change rules
goal: Gather every séimhiú and urú rule from this book, and learn to take a word's "hat" off to look it up in the dictionary.
bekal: say which words bring séimhiú and which bring urú
apply the right change without stopping to think
find the base form of a changed word so you can look it up in the dictionary

dialogs.title: Comhrá — An comhartha ar an mbóthar
dialogs.intro: Budi saw a sign at the entrance to a small town and asks Aoife about it after class.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A Aoife, chonaic mé comhartha inné: "Fáilte go dtí ár mBaile".
lines.id: Aoife, yesterday I saw a sign: "Welcome to our town".
lines.literal: O Aoife, saw I sign yesterday: "welcome to our town".

lines.text: Sin urú. "Baile" a bhí ann, agus chuir "ár" urú air.
lines.id: That's urú. The original word is "baile", and "ár" puts urú on it.

lines.literal: and what reason "my town" but "our town"?

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Mar go gcuireann "mo" séimhiú, agus "ár" urú. Sin an difríocht ar fad.

lines.text: Bain an hata den fhocal. "Bhean" — bain an h. "MBaile" — bain an m.

lines.text: Bain dhá litir: "fuil", ó "bí". Sin an ceann is deacra ar fad!

notes: **Séimhiú and urú aren't decoration — they carry meaning.** You saw the proof in Unit 8: *a theach*, *a teach*, and *a dteach* are all written with the same word *a*, and only the letter change tells you whether the house belongs to a man, a woman, or a group of people. Ignoring the letter changes means ignoring a large part of the grammar.

**The change always comes from the word in front.** It isn't the noun that "has" séimhiú; it's *mo*, *an*, *dhá*, *ar* that put it there. So the list to learn is the list of **triggers**, not of words — and there are only about twenty little trigger words, all of which you've already used in earlier units.

**Only seven letters can take urú.** *b, c, d, f, g, p, t* — plus vowels, which get *n-*. The letters *l, m, n, r, s* and the clusters *sc-, sm-, sp-, st-* are never touched by urú. For séimhiú it's nine letters: *b, c, d, f, g, m, p, s, t*.

**If you're unsure in conversation, keep talking.** Séimhiú and urú mistakes are the ones beginners make most, and native speakers still understand without any trouble. The proverb at the back of this book isn't just a pleasantry: *Is fearr Gaeilge bhriste ná Béarla cliste* — broken Irish is better than clever English.

blocks.text: Séimhiú inserts an **h** after the first letter. The nine letters that can take it: *b, c, d, f, g, m, p, s, t*.

blocks.title: When séimhiú doesn't happen even with a trigger
items: **After *an*, the letters *d* and *t* aren't softened.** *An deoch*, *an tine* — even though both are feminine.
**The letters *l, n, r* can never be softened.** *Mo lámh*, *níor labhair mé*, *rith mé*.
**The clusters *sc-, sm-, sp-, st-* aren't softened.** *Mo scoil*, *níor stop mé*, *an scoil*.
**Vowels aren't softened** — but *mo* and *do* shorten in front of them: *m'athair*, *d'aghaidh*.

blocks.text: Urú writes a new letter **in front of** the first letter, and the original letter stops being pronounced. The seven pairs: *mb, gc, nd, bhf, ng, bp, dt*. Vowels get *n-*.

blocks.title: Northern Irish uses séimhiú where others use urú
items: In Donegal and Ulster, *ar an mbord* often becomes *ar an bhord*, and *leis an gcaife* becomes *leis an chaife*.
This book uses urú because it is the form of *An Caighdeán Oifigiúil* and the one you'll meet most in books; the Ulster forms are widely accepted in use, though not standard.
If you learn from Ulster speakers and hear séimhiú where this book says urú, don't be confused — they aren't wrong.

sections.title: Taking a word's hat off — how to use the dictionary

blocks.text: Dictionaries store words in their bare form. If the word you're looking for isn't there, it's almost certainly wearing a hat. These three steps solve nine cases out of ten.

items: **Are the first two letters one of the urú pairs?** Drop the first letter. *MBaile* → *baile*. *Gcarr* → *carr*. *Ndoras* → *doras*. *Dteach* → *teach*. *Bpáiste* → *páiste*.
**Does it start with *bhf-*?** Drop **two** letters. *Bhfuil* → *fuil* (from the verb *bí*). *Bhfeiceann* → *feiceann* (from *feic*).
**Does it start with *d'*, *n-*, *t-*, or *h-*?** Drop that part along with the hyphen. *D'ól* → *ól*. *N-athair* → *athair*. *T-arán* → *arán*. *HÉireann* → *Éire*.

**Still can't find it?** The word may be a changed form of an irregular verb. Check the tables in Units 11, 17, and 18 — that's where *chuaigh*, *rinne*, *fuair*, *tugaim*, *deirim*, and *rachaidh* are hiding.
